# HBCB / PSD degradation-and-reuse chemistry

`hbcb-psd` · *Oohashi, Ueno, Maekawa, Kawai, Nishina & Honda, 2009; PSD model proposed by Oohashi et al. 1987*

*Also known as:* *hierarchical biomolecular covalent bond model*, *programmed self-decomposition model*

!!! warning "Archived: pruned"
    This entry is not part of the chemistry catalog (set aside from the catalog). It keeps its specification, generator and tests, and `generate_network` still runs it by id, but listings and the LLM tools leave it out. See the [catalog's archive](index.md#archive).

## Introduction

When an organism dies, its matter has to go somewhere. The usual explanation
is that it is broken down and reused through food chains. Tsutomu Oohashi and
colleagues proposed in 1987 a different emphasis, the **programmed self-decomposition (PSD) model**: the cells of
terrestrial organisms carry a built-in, genetically programmed mechanism that
takes the organism apart and hands its matter and its space back to the
environment. The hypothesis is biological. The artificial chemistry came later,
as one of the ways the group tested it.

In 2009 Oohashi, Ueno, Maekawa, Kawai, Nishina and Honda built on it a second
model, about the structure of the matter being decomposed, and used it to ask
*how far* self-decomposition should go. Their **hierarchical
biomolecular covalent bond (HBCB) model** arranges biomolecules in levels held
together by covalent bonds (the strong bonds that share electrons between
atoms): large biopolymers (BP, such as proteins or nucleic acids) are made of
biomonomers (BM, such as amino acids or nucleotides), which are themselves
made of smaller units, and so on down. Taking a protein apart into amino acids
leaves pieces a cell can reuse at once. Taking it apart further leaves
fragments that must first be rebuilt into amino acids. The paper's abstract
states the claim: organisms "have evolutionarily selected the PSD mechanism of
turning biological polymers (BPs) into biological monomers (BMs) as an
efficient biomolecular recycling strategy".

The 2009 study combined two kinds of evidence. Wet-lab experiments on living
organisms looked for a PSD mechanism. Simulations expressed different
self-decomposition processes as an artificial chemistry and let virtual
organisms that used them compete in a virtual ecosystem. Banzhaf and Yamamoto
summarise it in one paragraph of book §18.3.2, "Other AC Approaches to the
Modeling of Biochemical Pathways": "the virtual organisms able to break BP into
reusable BMs have an evolutionary advantage over other organisms that degrade
BPs into smaller units that are harder to recycle."

What Chemart holds is the chemistry only: a small, fixed hierarchy of
molecule classes with cleavage and synthesis reactions between neighbouring
levels, one programmed self-decomposition reaction, and a table of what it
costs to rebuild a biopolymer from each level. It is a static reaction network
with no kinetics, not the evolving ecosystem. The 2009 paper itself could not
be obtained (see *Implementation decisions*), so the hierarchy's size and
energies are parameters chosen by Chemart. Its neighbours in §18.3.2 are
[Tominaga's stackable strings](tominaga-stacked-strings.md) and
[Synthon](synthon.md), both constructive chemistries that model real
biochemistry in much more detail. The closest catalog entry in spirit is the
[Dorin and Korb ecosystem](dorin-korb-ecosystem.md), where organisms, atoms,
bonds and bond energies live in one simulated world and matter is recycled
through decay.

|---|---|
| **family** | systems-biology |
| **kind** | generator |
| **constructive** | no — fixed species set |

## How it works

### Classes of molecules

A species in this chemistry is not a particular molecule but a **class**, one
level of the hierarchy. With the default four levels, one family of
biomolecules has these classes, from the top down:

```
BP_0 | BP of family 0: 4 x BM_0; 64 base units
BM_0 | BM of family 0: 4 x C1_0; 16 base units
C1_0 | C1 of family 0: 4 x C0_0; 4 base units
C0_0 | C0 of family 0: base class, indivisible; 1 base units
```

`BP` is the biopolymer and `BM` the biomonomer, the two classes the model
names. Below them are unnamed lower classes: here `C1` and, at the bottom,
the base class `C0`, which cannot be split further (a taller hierarchy adds
`C2`, `C3` and so on). Each molecule of a class is
made of a fixed number of molecules of the class below (four here), so a
biopolymer contains 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 **base units**. The suffix `_0` is the
**family**: proteins and nucleic acids, say, would be two families, each with
its own hierarchy, and families never turn into each other. The default has
four families, which are identical copies.

### Reactions: hydrolysis down, synthesis up

Between each pair of neighbouring classes there are two reactions. For one
family the whole chemistry is these six:

```
BP_0 -> 4 BM_0
4 BM_0 -> BP_0
BM_0 -> 4 C1_0
4 C1_0 -> BM_0
C1_0 -> 4 C0_0
4 C0_0 -> C1_0
```

The downward reactions are **hydrolysis**, the cleavage of covalent bonds by
water, which is how cells break down proteins and nucleic acids. A molecule
falls apart into all its subunits at once; partial pieces are not modelled.
The upward reactions are **synthesis**, the reuse of the pieces to rebuild the
class above.

**Programmed self-decomposition** is one more reaction per family: the
organism's own regulated process that breaks a biopolymer down in a single
step to a chosen depth. By default the depth is BM, and then the PSD reaction
is simply `BP_0 -> 4 BM_0`, the hydrolysis step already in the list. A deeper
choice adds a reaction of its own, for example `BP_0 -> 16 C1_0` (one class
below BM) or `BP_0 -> 64 C0_0` (all the way to the base class).

### Bond energies

The HBCB model orders the hierarchy by the strength of its covalent bonds.
Chemart reads this as: the bonds that link monomers into a biopolymer are the
weakest, the ones hydrolysis cuts first, and bonds deeper inside a monomer are
progressively stronger. Each level therefore gets one **bond energy**, the
energy of one bond linking units of that level, and the values must decrease
strictly from the base class upwards. The default values, 4, 2 and 1 in
arbitrary units, are a Chemart choice, not published numbers.

A molecule of four subunits holds three bonds joining them, plus everything
inside the subunits. With the defaults, a `C1` holds 3 × 4 = 12 units of
bond energy, a `BM` 4 × 12 + 3 × 2 = 54, and a `BP` 4 × 54 + 3 × 1 = 219.

### The re-use cost

The model's claim is about what happens after decomposition: how much work it
takes to get back to a biopolymer. Chemart counts it for each class:

- From `BM`: one synthesis, `4 BM_0 -> BP_0`, which puts back 3 bonds of
  energy 1: **1 synthesis, energy 3**.
- From `C1`: four syntheses `4 C1_0 -> BM_0`, each putting back 3 bonds of
  energy 2, then the one above: **5 syntheses, energy 27**.
- From `C0`: sixteen syntheses `4 C0_0 -> C1_0` (16 × 3 × 4 = 192), then four
  and one as above: **21 syntheses, energy 219**, the whole bond energy of a
  biopolymer.

Stopping at BM is always the cheapest. This follows from the construction: the
route back from any deeper class passes through BM and then does the BM step
too, so it can only cost more, whatever the (positive) bond energies are. The
bond-energy ordering does not change which class wins; it only changes by how
much.

### Matter is conserved

Every reaction keeps the number of base units in each family unchanged: one
`BP_0` is worth 64, one `BM_0` 16, one `C1_0` 4, one `C0_0` 1. This is the
closed world of the model, in which matter is finite and recycled rather than
supplied from outside.

### What is not here

In the published work the chemistry is tested inside a virtual ecosystem,
where virtual organisms that use different self-decomposition processes
compete and evolve. Which decomposition depth wins is decided by that
competition, across organisms. One reaction network cannot express it, so Chemart does not
generate it, and it publishes no rates: every reaction's rate is `None`. The
network gives the structure (who turns into what, with what stoichiometry and
what bond energy) but no dynamics. To simulate it you would have to supply
rate laws yourself.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*implicit* — defined by a construction rule rather than listed). One class per level of the HBCB hierarchy, per family of biomolecules: the biopolymer BP at the top, the biomonomer BM directly below it, then the lower classes C(n-3) ... C0 down to the base class. A class-l molecule is `units_per_class` molecules of the class below, so a species is fixed by (family, level); its id is '&lt;class&gt;_&lt;family&gt;' (BP_0, BM_0, C1_0, C0_0) and its structure records the composition and the number of base units it contains.

The species set is finite and closed: the hierarchy is the closure of the cleavage rule from the biopolymers, so |S| = n_families x n_levels.

**R — reactions** (*implicit* — computed by an algorithm from the molecules that meet; molecules per reaction: 1, 4). Hydrolysis (cleavage) X_l -&gt; units_per_class X_(l-1) and its reverse, synthesis units_per_class X_(l-1) -&gt; X_l, between every pair of neighbouring classes; plus one programmed self-decomposition per family, BP -&gt; units_per_class^d X_t, which cleaves a biopolymer in one genetically regulated step down to the class named by psd_target (with psd_target = BM this is the single hydrolysis step, BP into BMs, that the paper's abstract calls one of the main processes of PSD).

The HBCB model orders the hierarchy by covalent bond energy: the BM-BM links of a biopolymer are the weakest bonds and the ones hydrolysis cleaves, and the bonds inside the lower classes are progressively stronger (enforced: bond_energies must decrease strictly upwards). Re-use is the synthesis direction, so the cost of returning to a BP grows with the depth of the decomposition.

**A — reactor**: `lattice-2d` (a two-dimensional grid on which only neighbours interact); or `well-stirred-multiset` (a well-stirred pot of discrete molecules that meet at random, with no notion of position).

*How the population is bounded:* Closed ecosystem: matter is finite and recycled, so there is no inflow or outflow and the base units of every family are conserved exactly.

The paper embeds the chemistry in a virtual ecosystem of competing organisms with mutation and finite matter; in the SIVA lineage of the same group (Sayama 1998) that ecosystem is a 256 x 256 lattice, periodic in x, with a temperature gradient along y and four finite substances, individuals occupying one pixel and carrying a chromosome (lifespan, optimal temperature, movement frequency, reproduction interval and the amount of each of the four substances needed to reproduce), and a decomposer module that returns the individual's matter to the environment. That level is a population of organisms, not one reaction network, and is not generated here.

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("hbcb-psd", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
hbcb-psd: 16 species, 24 reactions, status=complete
provides: energies, initial-state, mass-conservation, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: analysis, conservation, energies, hbcb, psd
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
BP_0 -> 4 BM_0
4 BM_0 -> BP_0
BM_0 -> 4 C1_0
4 C1_0 -> BM_0
C1_0 -> 4 C0_0
4 C0_0 -> C1_0
BP_1 -> 4 BM_1
4 BM_1 -> BP_1
… and 16 more
```

The default call above builds four identical families, 16 species and 24
reactions, with self-decomposition to BM. It reproduces no particular
published run, since none is available. With `n_families=1` the network is a
single hierarchy, which is easier to read:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("hbcb-psd", seed=1, n_families=1)
```

The seed makes no difference: nothing in this chemistry is random.

### Reading the result

The quantities the model is about are in `net.extras`:

```python
net.extras["analysis"]
# {'psd_target_class': 'BM',
#  'rebuild_cost_by_class': {'C0': {'syntheses_per_bp': 21, 'bond_energy_per_bp': 219.0},
#                            'C1': {'syntheses_per_bp': 5, 'bond_energy_per_bp': 27.0},
#                            'BM': {'syntheses_per_bp': 1, 'bond_energy_per_bp': 3.0}},
#  'recyclable': True}
net.extras["psd"]
# {'target': 'BM', 'reactions': ['BP_0 -> 4 BM_0']}
net.extras["energies"]
# {'C0_0': 0.0, 'C1_0': 12.0, 'BM_0': 54.0, 'BP_0': 219.0}
net.extras["hbcb"]["bond_energy_per_link"]
# {'C1_0': 4.0, 'BM_0': 2.0, 'BP_0': 1.0}
net.extras["conservation"]
# [{'name': 'base units of family 0',
#   'vector': {'C0_0': 1, 'C1_0': 4, 'BM_0': 16, 'BP_0': 64}}]
```

- `analysis.rebuild_cost_by_class` is the re-use cost of the previous section,
  for every class below BP. `recyclable` is `True` only when self-decomposition
  stops at BM.
- `psd` names the self-decomposition reaction.
- `energies` is the total bond energy inside one molecule of each class;
  `hbcb.bond_energy_per_link` is the energy of one bond that links subunits
  into the named class.
- `conservation` holds one law per family: the weights that make the total
  number of base units constant.
- `net.initial_state` puts `initial_bp` biopolymers (8 by default) of each
  family in the pot and nothing else, an amount Chemart chose.

### Comparing decomposition depths

`psd_target` selects the depth, which is what the published simulations
compared. Over its four values, with one family:

```
psd_target  reactions  PSD reaction        recyclable
none        6          (none)              False
BM          6          BP_0 -> 4 BM_0      True
sub-BM      7          BP_0 -> 16 C1_0     False
base        7          BP_0 -> 64 C0_0     False
```

`none` is an organism that does not decompose itself: only the plain
hydrolysis and synthesis reactions remain. `sub-BM` needs at least three
levels.

### A deeper hierarchy

`n_levels`, `units_per_class` and `bond_energies` set the shape of the
hierarchy; `bond_energies` needs `n_levels - 1` strictly decreasing, positive
entries, or generation raises `ValueError`. Six levels of three units each:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("hbcb-psd", n_levels=6, units_per_class=3,
                               bond_energies=[16, 8, 4, 2, 1], n_families=1)
net.extras["analysis"]["rebuild_cost_by_class"]
# {'C0': {'syntheses_per_bp': 121, 'bond_energy_per_bp': 3110.0},
#  'C1': {'syntheses_per_bp': 40,  'bond_energy_per_bp': 518.0},
#  'C2': {'syntheses_per_bp': 13,  'bond_energy_per_bp': 86.0},
#  'C3': {'syntheses_per_bp': 4,   'bond_energy_per_bp': 14.0},
#  'BM': {'syntheses_per_bp': 1,   'bond_energy_per_bp': 2.0}}
```

The cost of returning grows quickly with depth: each level down multiplies the
number of syntheses by roughly `units_per_class`. All settings generate
instantly.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `n_levels` | `int` | `4` | structural | number of classes in the HBCB hierarchy, from the base class up to the biopolymer; the top class is BP, the one below it BM, and the rest are the lower classes C(n-3) ... C0 <br>`2` … `10` |
| `units_per_class` | `int` | `4` | structural | molecules of class l-1 in one molecule of class l; a BP therefore holds units_per_class^(n_levels-1) base units <br>`2` … `8` |
| `n_families` | `int` | `4` | structural | independent families of biomolecules, each with its own hierarchy (proteins, nucleic acids, ...); families do not interconvert <br>`1` … `8` · *range:* the SIVA ecosystem of the same group (Sayama 1998, fig. 3 and table 1) holds four finite substances; the number used in the 2009 paper is not known |
| `psd_target` | `enum` | `BM` | selection | depth of the programmed self-decomposition: 'BM' cleaves a BP to biomonomers, which can be re-used directly (the species the paper finds superior); 'sub-BM' one class below BM and 'base' all the way to the base class, both of which have to be rebuilt through every intermediate class; 'none' is a species that does not self-decompose <br>one of `none`, `BM`, `sub-BM`, `base` |
| `bond_energies` | `list` | `[4.0, 2.0, 1.0]` | thermodynamic | energy of one covalent bond at each level of the hierarchy, entry i being the bonds that link class-i units into a class-(i+1) molecule; needs n_levels - 1 entries and must decrease strictly, the HBCB ordering (deeper bonds are stronger, the BM-BM links of a BP weakest). The ordering is the model; the numbers are a Chemart default |
| `initial_bp` | `int` | `8` | population | biopolymers of each family present at the start, the matter of the closed ecosystem (initial_state); the paper gives no amounts <br>`0` … `1000000` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "11 decisions"

    - The 2009 paper (book ref [643]) could not be obtained. It is bronze open access on MIT Press, but direct.mit.edu answers both curl and WebFetch with a Cloudflare challenge / HTTP 403; the Internet Archive (Wayback and its CDX API) was globally offline during this session; Springer, ingenta and every other indexed location are closed access; Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, CORE, OpenAIRE, fatcat and CiNii list no other full text. The implementation therefore follows book 18.3.2 and the paper's published abstract, which is why fidelity is book+decisions and not reconstructed. Everything below that the abstract and the book do not state is a Chemart reconstruction.
    - From the abstract and the book, the model's content is: biomolecules are arranged hierarchically by the energy of their covalent bonds (HBCB); self-decomposition is a genetically regulated, endergonic process whose main step is hydrolysis, which decomposes a BP into BMs; and virtual species whose self-decomposition cleaves a BP to BMs are evolutionarily superior to species that cleave it into classes lower than BM. The depth of decomposition is therefore the parameter the model compares (psd_target), and the advantage is a re-use cost, which is what extras.analysis reports.
    - The number of classes, the branching factor units_per_class, and which concrete biomolecules sit at each class are not known from the abstract; they are parameters (n_levels, units_per_class), with only BP and BM named as the model names them. The lower classes are written C(n-3) ... C0 rather than given chemical identities.
    - Bond energies: the HBCB ordering (bonds deeper in the hierarchy are stronger, the BM-BM links of a biopolymer weakest, so hydrolysis cleaves them first) is the model and is enforced - bond_energies must decrease strictly upwards or generation raises ValueError. The numeric default [4.0, 2.0, 1.0] is a Chemart choice and is not a published value. A molecule's total bond energy (extras.energies) is accumulated down the hierarchy, a class-l molecule being units_per_class class-(l-1) molecules joined by units_per_class - 1 bonds; that arithmetic is also a Chemart convention.
    - Each class-l molecule is treated as exactly units_per_class molecules of the class below, and cleavage as complete (a molecule falls apart into all its subunits at once, matching 'hydrolysis decomposes a BP into BMs'). Partial oligomers are not modelled: the paper's cleavage pattern is not known, and inventing one would invent chemistry.
    - Programmed self-decomposition is one reaction per family, BP -&gt; units_per_class^d X_t, the organism's single genetically regulated process; the stepwise cleavages of the hierarchy are present as the chemistry in their own right. With psd_target = 'BM' the two coincide, and the PSD reaction is that same hydrolysis reaction rather than a duplicate.
    - No kinetics are published, so every rate is None and the entry provides no rate-constants; the fact that PSD is endergonic and genetically regulated is recorded in the notes rather than turned into a rate law or an energy barrier.
    - The ecosystem is closed (no inflow or outflow): the book calls it a virtual ecosystem with recycling and the SIVA lineage gives it finite matter, so the base units of each family are conserved exactly (extras.conservation, one law per family, the vector being units_per_class^level). initial_bp is a Chemart amount; the paper gives none.
    - Selection between decomposition strategies acts across competing organisms and cannot live inside one reaction network, so it is not generated. The cost of returning to a biopolymer from each class (number of syntheses and covalent bond energy per BP) is reported in extras.analysis.rebuild_cost_by_class instead, and that is the quantity in which decomposing to BM is optimal. The v1 parameters bond_hierarchy (type matrix) and decomposition_strategy become bond_energies and psd_target.
    - v1 said constructive: true. The species set is finite, closed and known from the parameters (|S| = n_families x n_levels: the closure of the cleavage rule terminates at the base class), so it is corrected to false.
    - n_families defaults to 4 because the SIVA ecosystem of the same group holds four finite substances (Sayama 1998); the 2009 paper's number is unknown, and the families do not interact, so this only replicates the hierarchy.

## Results

### The 2009 study: why stopping at monomers wins

Oohashi et al. (2009) is the work the book cites. It could not be obtained for
Chemart, so what it found is known here only from its published abstract and
the book's summary; no numbers, figures or simulation settings are available.
According to the abstract:

- Biological experiments "have shown that terrestrial life possesses a PSD
  mechanism as an endergonic, genetically regulated process" (endergonic: it
  consumes energy rather than releasing it), and that "hydrolysis, which
  decomposes a BP into BMs, is one of the main processes of such a mechanism".
  The paper's database indexing lists the protozoan *Tetrahymena pyriformis*
  as an organism studied.
- In the simulations, "the virtual species in which the self-decomposition
  process mainly involved covalent bond cleavage from a BP to BMs showed
  evolutionary superiority over other species in which the self-decomposition
  process involved cleavage from BP to classes lower than BM."

The authors conclude that the two kinds of evidence "strongly support the
existence of PSD and the validity and effectiveness of the HBCB model". The
book presents this as an artificial chemistry built to study "the emergence of
biochemical pathways for the degradation and reuse of biomolecular compounds".

**What Chemart reproduces.** Not the evolutionary result itself, since that
needs the competing population. Chemart reproduces the reason the book gives
for it, that monomers are easier to recycle, as the re-use cost: from BM one
synthesis gets back to a biopolymer, while every deeper class needs strictly
more syntheses and strictly more bond energy. The tests check this for the
default network (1 synthesis from BM against 5 and 21, energy 3 against 27 and
219), for hierarchies of two to six levels, and for generated networks with
three and five levels. As explained above, this ranking holds by construction;
it is a restatement of the argument, not an independent confirmation of it.

The other published features are built into the network and tested as such:

- **Bonds ordered by energy, BM–BM links weakest.** The tests check the
  default per-bond energies (4, 2, 1 from the base upwards), the accumulated
  energy of each class (12, 54, 219), and that increasing, equal or zero
  energies are rejected. The abstract says only that biomolecules are arranged
  "according to the energy strength of their covalent bonds"; the direction of
  the ordering is Chemart's reading, taken from the fact that hydrolysis
  cleaves the BM–BM links.
- **Finite, recycled matter.** The tests check that the network has no inflow
  or outflow and that the stoichiometry conserves each family's base units
  (weights 64, 16, 4, 1).
- **Hydrolysis of a BP into BMs.** The tests check the exact reaction list,
  that PSD to BM is the same reaction as that hydrolysis and not a duplicate,
  that deeper targets add `BP_0 -> 16 C1_0` or `BP_0 -> 64 C0_0`, and that
  `none` adds nothing.

### The earlier ecosystem: SIVA

The evolving ecosystem Chemart leaves out has an earlier, documented relative.
Sayama (1998, in Japanese) built SIVA-2r, a parallel simulator of virtual
organisms, to test the PSD model. Its world is a 256 × 256 grid, wrapping
around left to right, with a temperature gradient from top to bottom and four
kinds of finite substance. Each organism occupies one cell and carries a
chromosome with genes for lifespan, optimal temperature, how often it moves,
how often it reproduces, and how much of each of the four substances it needs
to reproduce. Mutations arise when a gene is copied. Organisms of the
self-decomposing kind (Oohashi's "self-reproduction–self-decomposition"
system: von Neumann's self-reproducing automaton with its extra module
replaced by a decomposer module) take themselves apart when their lifespan
ends or the temperature is wrong for them, returning their substances and their cell to the environment.
The non-decomposing kind (von Neumann's automaton unchanged) never return
anything, and simply stop when the temperature is wrong.

Sayama ran both kinds at 13 mutation rates, from 2⁰ down to 2⁻²⁴ per gene
copy, 10 random seeds each: 2 × 13 × 10 = 260 runs of 5,000 steps, measuring
the number of living organisms. At fairly low mutation rates the two differed
sharply. The non-decomposing population stopped growing and evolving once it
had used up the space and matter. The self-decomposing population kept
reproducing in the same restored environment, gathered more chances to
mutate, and eventually produced species adapted to a range of temperature
zones even at low mutation rates.

This experiment compares self-decomposition against none, not decomposition
to BM against deeper decomposition, so it is not the 2009 result. Chemart does
not reproduce it either. It is described here because it is the only
published PSD ecosystem available to this page, and the source of Chemart's
choice of four families of biomolecules, after SIVA's four substances.

### Later work

Citation databases list later papers by the same group that build on the PSD
model, on the evolution of a genetic program for death and on "mortal" versus
"immortal" organisms (see *Further reading*). They were not read for this
page, and the book does not discuss them.

IPSJ Transactions 39(6):1782-1789 (in Japanese), open access: https://ipsj.ixsq.nii.ac.jp/record/13055/files/IPSJ-JNL3906025.pdf - the SIVA-2r ecosystem: Oohashi et al.'s self-reproduction~self-decomposition (SRSD) system as von Neumann's automaton with a decomposer module FZ (figs. 1-2), the 256x256 lattice with a temperature gradient and four finite substances, the chromosome genes (table 1), and the result that self-decomposing populations keep adapting while non-decomposing ones stagnate once space and matter are used up (figs. 10-11, 2 x 13 x 10 = 260 runs over 13 mutation rates).

### Further reading

- Oohashi, T., Nakata, D., Kikuchi, T. & Murakami, K. (1987). "Programmed
  self-decomposition model" (プログラムされた自己解体モデル). *Kagaku Kisoron
  Kenkyu* (科学基礎論研究) 18(2):79–87. In Japanese. The original PSD
  hypothesis, as cited by Sayama (1998); not read for this page.
- Oohashi, T., Maekawa, T., Ueno, O., Kawai, N., Nishina, E. & Shimohara, K.
  (2001). Artificial life based on the programmed self-decomposition model,
  SIVA. *Artificial Life and Robotics* 5(2):77–87.
  <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02481343>. Not read for this page.
- Later papers of the group, listed by Semantic Scholar as citing the 2009

  the origin of an altruistic gene", *Artificial Life*,
  <https://doi.org/10.1162/ARTL_a_00098>;
